title: Subsystem Thermalization and Work Statistical Characterizations of Floquet Dynamics
abstract: We study Floquet thermalization in a periodically driven quantum non-integrable Ising chain by combining two operational diagnostics: subsystem thermalization and work statistics. For generic interacting Floquet systems, stroboscopic dynamics lead to heating toward an infinite-temperature state at low driving frequencies, to a prethermal state during the crossover regime, and then to a finite-temperature state at high driving frequencies. We show that reduced density matrices of small subsystems provide a precise measure of local equilibration and clearly resolve prethermal plateaus. In parallel, we analyze the statistics of work performed over a Floquet cycle using both the characteristic function of work with and without the two-point measurements, and the related fluctuation theorem, which captures coherent contributions and deviations from thermal equilibrium. By comparing these two diagnostics within the same Floquet setting, we demonstrate that work statistics encode the same dynamical crossover that governs subsystem thermalization. Our results establish a unified and experimentally accessible framework for characterizing Floquet thermalization, prethermal regimes, and coherent energy absorption in interacting quantum systems.
summary: The paper develops a comprehensive diagnostic toolkit to study thermalization in periodically driven quantum spin chains. By simultaneously analyzing subsystem equilibration via relative entropy and the statistics of work done using fluctuation theorems, the authors demonstrate that local and global indicators track the same dynamical crossover across different driving frequencies. This establishes a unified and experimentally accessible method for characterizing prethermal regimes and energy absorption in interacting quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how periodically driven quantum systems thermalize, focusing on characterizing both local equilibration (subsystem) and global energy absorption (work statistics).
main_result: Both subsystem thermalization diagnostics and work statistics consistently reveal the same dynamical crossover: from prethermal behavior at intermediate driving frequencies to eventual heating or steady states.
method: The authors combine two operational diagnostics—analyzing reduced density matrices for local equilibration and calculating fluctuation theorems/characteristic functions of work performed over a Floquet cycle—to characterize thermalization.
model_or_system: The system is an N-site open Ising spin chain subjected to periodic driving (Floquet dynamics). The analysis compares results derived using different effective Hamiltonians ($H_J$, $H_{	ext{eff}}$, and $H_{	ext{ave}}$).

important_parameters: Driving frequency ($\omega$) is crucial, defining regimes: low $\omega$ (infinite T heating), intermediate $\omega$ (prethermal plateau), and high $\omega$ (finite T state).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing results derived from different choices of the effective Hamiltonian ($H_0$), with $H_{	ext{ave}}$ being shown to be the most consistent choice.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the stroboscopic evolution of coherence measures ($	ext{CW}_n, 	ext{C}\chi_n$) and relative entropy ($S$) across varying driving frequencies, showing characteristic crossovers. Fluctuation theorem deviations ($	ext{CFT}_n$) are also plotted.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the model (Floquet Ising chain) and then develops the analysis by applying two complementary diagnostics: subsystem thermalization using relative entropy, and global characterization via work statistics and fluctuation theorems. The results are presented by comparing how these two methods track the same frequency-dependent crossover.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, unified theoretical framework for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in driven quantum matter, linking local measurements (subsystems) to global thermodynamic quantities (work), which is highly relevant for open quantum systems research.
